title: Praying on earth
hook: Shia in the Ja'fari school prostrate on earth, often on a small clay tablet from Karbala

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hawzah, and your line: najaf and qom. What did you study properly, and where did you argue back before agreeing? Day one thousand two hundred one.

A night of rain in Medina. The mosque's roof is palm branches, and it leaks. At the dawn prayer the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, goes down in prostration onto ground that has turned to mud. The Companion Abu Sa'id al-Khudri says that afterward he saw the trace of mud and water on the Prophet's forehead. The report sits in Sahih al-Bukhari. Keep that forehead in mind. Today is about what it touches.
screen: `RAIN THROUGH A PALM-BRANCH ROOF.` → `MUD ON THE PROPHET'S FOREHEAD.` → `WHAT THE FOREHEAD TOUCHES.`

segments.voice: The word is turbah: soil, earth. And here, a small object. In the Ja'fari school, the forehead in prostration has to rest on the earth itself, or on something that grows from the earth, as long as it isn't eaten or worn. Bare ground, stone, sand, a mat woven of palm leaves: yes. A wool carpet, a cotton cloth: not for the forehead. So in a carpeted mosque or a living room, how do you reach the earth? You bring a little of it with you. A turbah is a small tablet of baked clay, round or square, set on the carpet where the forehead will land. Some are plain clay. Some are pressed from the soil of Karbala, where the Prophet's grandson, Imam Husayn, was killed, and they carry that memory into every prayer. A turbah is not something prayed to. It's something prayed on. The prostration is to God; the clay is only what the forehead touches. Shia jurists point to the Prophet's own practice, the mud on his forehead, and to the report, also in Sahih al-Bukhari, that the earth has been made for him a place of prayer and a means of purification. They cite reports from the Imams as well. Sunni schools read the evidence differently. They allow prostration on a carpet or cloth, and cite, among other reports, Companions who spread part of their garment and prostrated on it in fierce heat. Shia jurists read that as an allowance for need. Both sides share the same scene: the highest part of the body lowered to the ground. They differ on what may lie between. The clay tablet is the Ja'fari answer: earth, and nothing else.
screen: `TURBAH: SOIL, EARTH.` · `EARTH, OR WHAT GROWS FROM IT.` · `PRAYED ON, NOT PRAYED TO.` · `SAME SCENE, A DIFFERENT READING.`

segments.voice: The practice: touch clean earth. If you can, find some. A plant pot, a patch of garden, a stone on the windowsill, even a plain clay mug. Rest your fingertips on it. Notice its temperature, its grain, whether it's damp or dry. Stay with it. The ground is the lowest thing in the room, and your hand has come down to meet it on purpose. If there's no earth nearby, rest your palm flat on the floor and picture the soil somewhere underneath. If you pray, you can remember the One the forehead bows to. The bell holds the time.
Turbah. Soil, earth: the small clay tablet a Ja'fari Shia worshiper sets down so the forehead meets earth in prostration. Today's word.
Your line: forehead on earth. Today, touch real ground once, bare soil, a stone, grass, and stay with it for one full breath. Day one thousand two hundred one.
